graph.definition: A structure made of a set of vertices and a set of edges, where each edge connects two vertices. In this module graphs are finite and simple: no edge connects a vertex to itself, and at most one edge connects a pair of vertices — one per direction when the graph is directed. A graph may be directed or undirected and weighted or unweighted.

vertex.definition: A basic element of a graph, drawn as a circle. Also called a node.

edge.definition: A connection between two distinct vertices. In an undirected graph it can be followed in both directions; in a directed graph only from its tail to its head, and it is then also called an arc.

neighbor.definition: A vertex is a neighbor of another when an edge connects them.

path.definition: A sequence of vertices in which each consecutive pair is connected by an edge. Its length is the number of edges it contains.

cycle.definition: A path that starts and ends at the same vertex, uses at least three edges and repeats no other vertex.

traversal.definition: A systematic process that visits every vertex reachable from a starting vertex exactly once.

bfs.definition: A traversal that uses a queue to visit vertices in order of their distance from the starting vertex, measured in number of edges.

dfs.definition: A traversal that follows edges as deep as possible from the most recently discovered vertex, backtracking when no undiscovered neighbor remains. It can be implemented recursively or with an explicit stack.

queue.definition: A first-in, first-out (FIFO) collection: elements are removed in the same order in which they were added.

stack.definition: A last-in, first-out (LIFO) collection: the most recently added element is removed first.

frontier.definition: The data structure holding the vertices the traversal still has to work on: the queue in BFS, the stack in DFS.

connectedComponent.definition: A maximal set of vertices in which every pair is connected by a path. A traversal from a starting vertex reaches exactly the vertices of that vertex's connected component.

isolatedVertex.definition: A vertex with no edges. It forms a connected component on its own.

startVertex.definition: The vertex where a traversal begins.

undiscovered.definition: State of a vertex the traversal has not yet reached.

discovered.definition: State of a vertex the traversal has reached and added to the frontier, but has not yet started processing.

processing.definition: State of a vertex whose neighbors the traversal has started, but not finished, examining.

processed.definition: State of a vertex whose neighbors have all been examined. The traversal does not return to it.

visited.definition: General term for a vertex the traversal has reached. Because it is ambiguous, this lab distinguishes discovered, processing and processed vertices.

shortestPath.definition: A path between two vertices whose total weight is as small as possible. In an unweighted graph that is the path with the fewest edges, which BFS finds; with weights it is Dijkstra, Bellman–Ford or Floyd–Warshall that finds it, and a reachable negative cycle means no shortest path exists.

weight.definition: The number carried by an edge, read as a cost, a length or a time. In an unweighted graph every edge counts as 1.

minimumSpanningTree.definition: A spanning tree whose total weight is as small as possible. Kruskal and Prim both build one. On a disconnected graph there is none: the result is a minimum spanning forest, one tree per component.

floydWarshall.definition: An algorithm for the shortest paths between every pair of vertices. It takes each vertex in turn as a pivot and asks whether a detour through it shortens any path.

prim.definition: An algorithm for a minimum spanning tree: grow one tree from a start vertex, always adding the cheapest edge that leaves it.

kruskal.definition: An algorithm for a minimum spanning tree: take the edges from the lightest to the heaviest and keep each one that joins two different components.

disjointSet.definition: A structure that keeps elements divided into separate groups: find reports the group of an element, union merges two groups. Kruskal uses it to tell whether an edge would close a cycle.

directedGraph.definition: A graph whose edges have a direction: an edge from u to v can be followed only that way. The same pair may carry one edge in each direction.

undirectedGraph.definition: A graph whose edges have no direction: each edge can be followed from either of its two vertices.

weightedGraph.definition: A graph in which every edge carries a number, its weight. Weights may be negative.

arc.definition: An edge of a directed graph, taken in its own direction, from its tail to its head.

spanningTree.definition: A set of edges of an undirected graph that connects every vertex and contains no cycle. It always has exactly one edge fewer than the number of vertices.

topologicalOrder.definition: An order of the vertices of a directed graph in which every arc points forward. It exists exactly when the graph has no directed cycle.

dag.definition: A directed graph with no directed cycle. These are exactly the graphs that have a topological order.

inDegree.definition: The number of arcs pointing into a vertex. A vertex of in-degree 0 has nothing that must come before it.

relaxation.definition: Examining an arc from u to w to see whether going through u reaches w more cheaply than the distance recorded so far, and lowering that distance when it does. It is the single operation behind Dijkstra and Bellman–Ford.

negativeCycle.definition: A cycle whose weights add up to less than zero. Going round it again always lowers the total, so no shortest path exists through it; Bellman–Ford detects one.

unionFind.definition: A structure that keeps a collection of disjoint sets and answers, quickly, whether two elements are in the same set, and joins two sets. Kruskal uses it to tell whether an edge would close a cycle.

settled.definition: In Dijkstra, a vertex whose distance is final and will not change again.

dijkstra.definition: An algorithm for the shortest paths from one start vertex in a graph with no negative weight. It repeatedly settles the nearest vertex that is not settled yet.

bellmanFord.definition: An algorithm for the shortest paths from one start vertex that also accepts negative weights. It relaxes every arc n − 1 times and then detects a reachable negative cycle.

kahn.definition: An algorithm for a topological order: repeatedly take a vertex of in-degree 0 and remove its outgoing arcs. If vertices remain when none is left, the graph has a cycle.
